![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/generate/scratch/17592186087824/plots/shift-stretch-v5/33db6f04179abc5823826daa1d4a3236f7f741a7d6f08f2756dadfe0973a76e7.png)

The graph above shows $y=k({2}^{x})+c.$ Find the value of $k$ and $c.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The horizontal asymptote of the curve $y=k({2}^{x})+c$ is $y=c.$ In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=-2,$ so $c=-2.$

Therefore, our function takes the form

$$
y=k({2}^{x})-2.
$$

We can solve for $k$ by finding a point on the graph and substituting for $x$ and $y.$ The labeled point on the graph is $(0,0),$ so we substitute $x=0$ and $y=0$ into the function and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =k({2}^{x})-2 \\ 0 & =k({2}^{0})-2 \\ 0 & =k(1)-2 \\ 0 & =k-2 \\ 2 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=2$ and $c=-2.$
